title: The attributes
hook: one verse says nothing is like Him, and in the same breath calls Him the Hearer, the Seer

segments.voice: Yesterday: why suffering, and a wisdom not always seen, with tears and trust side by side.

One sentence of the Qur'an, in two halves. The first half, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness." Nothing is like Him. Then, in the same breath: "and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Hearing and seeing are things you do. A child does them. A cat does them. So the verse that says nothing is like Allah goes straight on to describe Him with words we use for ourselves. That isn't a slip. It's the whole problem of this part in one line.
screen: `NAUGHT IS AS HIS LIKENESS.` → `AND HE IS THE HEARER, THE SEER.` → `BOTH IN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Day 232 gave you the most beautiful names; today, how theologians speak of them. The Arabic word is sifat, attributes: the qualities Allah describes Himself with, knowing, willing, powerful, living, hearing, seeing, speaking. Another verse says: "Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them." So Muslims call on Him by what He has said of Himself. But how do you use those words without shrinking Him to our size? Theologians name two ditches beside the road. One is tashbih, likening: hearing like ours, only bigger, with ears and a place to stand. The other is ta'til, emptying out: deciding the words mean nothing at all. The road runs between, and each school we've met walks it its own way. The Atharis affirm hearing and seeing as they came, and don't ask how. The Ash'aris and Maturidis affirm a set of attributes as real and eternal, set out by argument, and explain some other descriptions with care. The Mu'tazilah, guarding oneness, said Allah knows and hears by His very essence, not by attributes added to Him. And Shia theology has its own careful version of that concern. Different routes, one shared fence: He is not like His creation. As theologians put it, He hears, but not with ears. He sees, but not with eyes. The word hearing is true of Him; the picture that comes with it isn't.
screen: `SIFAT: WHAT HE SAYS OF HIMSELF.` · `TWO DITCHES: LIKENING, EMPTYING.` · `EACH SCHOOL WALKS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `HE HEARS, NOT WITH EARS.`

segments.voice: Listen, and loosely count the sounds you can hear, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and notice how few you can hold at once: that's our hearing, limited and needing ears. Now hold the word the verse uses, the Hearer, without building a picture: hearing without any of those limits, and without our shape. If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, as-Sami'; if you don't, let the phrase nothing like Him be enough.
Sifat. The attributes of Allah: hearing, seeing, knowing, willing and more, affirmed without likening Him to anything. Today's word.
Your line: nothing like him. Real names, and no picture big enough to hold them. Go gently.

howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah by His names and attributes, such as as-Sami', the Hearer, and al-Basir, the Seer, while holding with Qur'an 42:11 that nothing is like Him; the schools of theology explain the attributes in different ways.

fork.setup: the Qur'an calls Allah the Hearer. how do the theologians want you to take it?
options: real hearing, but not with ears, and like nothing in creation.
just a figure of speech that means nothing.
fork.reveal: the verse holds both: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer. The schools differ in how they explain it, but all avoid likening Him to creation.

chat.says: Why does one verse say nothing is like Allah, then call Him the Hearer?
options: To affirm real names while keeping Him unlike anything we picture.
Because the second half describes the Prophet, not Allah Himself.
Because the second half describes the angels who record deeds.
chat.meaning: The verse holds both: real names and attributes, and nothing like Him. He hears, but not with ears; the word is true, the picture isn't.
